title: Introduction to HTML
subtitle: Understand the web and build your first webpage
description: Learn what HTML really does, how browsers interpret markup, how tags and elements work, how attributes provide information, and how to build a complete HTML document.

blocks.text: Welcome! Let's build your first webpage

Welcome to your first HTML lesson! Before we begin, I want you to understand something important: you do not need to know everything about computers to become a capable web developer. You need curiosity, practice, patience, and the willingness to understand why your code works. I will guide you through the ideas step by step. Please do not rush. When you see an example, pause and try to predict what it will do before reading the explanation.

Imagine you want to create a learning website. It needs a title, paragraphs, pictures, links, buttons, and different sections. How would you tell a browser which words form a heading and which words form a paragraph? You need a language for describing the structure and meaning of that content. That is where HTML comes in. By the end of this lesson, you will understand the foundation of a webpage and will have built a complete document yourself.
Section 1 — How a webpage reaches your screen

Let's start with something familiar. When you open a website in Chrome, you are using a web browser. A browser is software that requests, reads, and displays web content. Other browsers include Firefox, Safari, and Edge. A website may store its files on a computer called a web server. When you visit the website, your browser can request those files and receive a response. The browser then interprets the returned HTML and other resources to display the page.

A simple webpage can be created as a local file on your device. You can write the HTML in a code editor, save it with an .html extension, and open it in a browser. You do not need to publish a website or buy a domain before you begin learning. A domain is a human-readable address, such as example.com. Hosting is a service that makes website files available over a network. These ideas become important when you are ready to publish your projects, but first you can learn by building pages locally.

Three technologies often work together on a website. HTML describes the structure and meaning of content. CSS controls how that content looks, including colors, spacing, borders, and layout. JavaScript adds behavior, such as responding when someone clicks a button or enters information into a form. Think of a building: HTML describes its rooms and doors, CSS influences its appearance, and JavaScript can make interactive systems respond. This comparison is not perfect, but it helps you remember the different responsibilities.

Look carefully at that first example. It contains plain text rather than HTML elements. A browser can still display it, but the document does not explicitly identify the text as a heading, paragraph, or other meaningful element. HTML becomes much more useful when you mark content according to its purpose. In the next section, you will learn how those marks work. If your editor offers an HTML preview, try the sample there and observe the result.

blocks.question: You are building a webpage with a heading, a blue background, and a button that reacts when clicked. Which division of responsibilities is most appropriate?
options: HTML defines the heading and background, CSS handles the click, and JavaScript defines the page structure.
HTML structures the heading and button, CSS styles the background, and JavaScript handles the click behavior.
CSS creates the document structure, HTML handles the click, and JavaScript changes only text colors.
JavaScript must create every element, because HTML cannot display content without CSS.
blocks.explanation: HTML describes the structure and meaning of the heading and button. CSS controls presentation, including the background color. JavaScript can respond to a click. These technologies can work together without having to do one another's jobs.
blocks.hint: Separate structure, appearance, and interactive behavior.

blocks.text: Section 2 — What HTML means and why markup matters

HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language. HyperText refers to text connected to other resources through links. Markup means adding recognizable markers that describe parts of a document. Language means it follows defined rules that browsers understand. HTML is not a general-purpose programming language like JavaScript or Python: HTML alone does not provide the usual programming tools for variables, loops, or decision-making. Its main purpose is to describe document content and structure.

Imagine writing the word Welcome in a file. The browser can display those letters, but the word alone does not explicitly tell the browser whether it is the main heading, a paragraph, or a button label. Now compare

Welcome

with

Welcome

. The first marks the text as a level-one heading. The second marks it as a paragraph. The visible word is the same, but the meaning and default presentation are different. This is one of the most important ideas in HTML: choose elements according to what the content means.

HTML is read by the browser as markup, not as ordinary text that should all appear on the screen. The browser interprets tags and uses them to construct a document structure, often represented internally as a tree of elements. This structure allows browsers, assistive technologies, and scripts to understand relationships between pieces of content. For example, a heading followed by paragraphs creates a meaningful section that is easier to navigate than a page made entirely from generic containers.

You will meet many elements as you progress. Headings use h1 through h6. Paragraphs use p. Links use a. Images use img. Lists use elements such as ul, ol, and li. Buttons use button. Forms use elements such as form, label, input, and select. You do not need to memorise every element today. Focus on understanding the pattern: the element you choose communicates the role of the content.

blocks.title: Sample 2 — Give content meaningful structure
blocks.code:
My Learning Journey

I am learning to build webpages.

My First Goal

I want to understand HTML before adding advanced features.
blocks.output:
My Learning Journey
I am learning to build webpages.
My First Goal
I want to understand HTML before adding advanced features.

blocks.text: Notice that h1 and h2 are both headings, but they represent different levels. Use h1 for the main heading of the page or main content, and use lower-level headings to organise subsections logically. Do not choose a heading level simply because its default font size looks attractive. You can change the appearance later with CSS. Correct structure helps people understand your content and helps assistive technologies navigate it.

blocks.question: A developer wants the words 'Account Settings' to identify a major section, followed by a smaller subsection called 'Privacy'. Which markup communicates the hierarchy most clearly?
options:
Account Settings

Privacy

Account Settings

Privacy

, because paragraph elements always create heading hierarchy.

Account Settings

Privacy
<title>Account Settings</title><title>Privacy</title> inside the visible page body.
blocks.explanation: A level-one heading followed by a level-two heading communicates that Privacy is a subsection of Account Settings. Paragraphs do not create heading hierarchy, and title belongs in the document head rather than being used as a visible body heading.
blocks.hint: Choose elements that express the relationship between the main section and its subsection.

blocks.text: Section 3 — Tags, elements, and nesting

Let's make three terms clear: tag, element, and attribute. A tag is markup such as

or

. An opening tag begins an element, while a closing tag usually marks where that element ends. An element includes the opening tag, its content, and its closing tag when the element uses that pattern. For example, in

Learning is a process.

, the complete paragraph is the element, and the text between the tags is its content.

Most ordinary text elements have an opening tag and a closing tag. The closing tag uses a slash before the element name, as in

. Forgetting a closing tag can cause unexpected results, particularly when elements are nested. Browsers often try to recover from mistakes, so a page may appear to work even when the markup is incorrect. Do not use that as a reason to ignore structure. Learn to write clear, properly nested HTML from the beginning.

Nesting means placing one element inside another. In

Learn HTML carefully.

, the strong element is inside the paragraph. Its content is marked as strongly important. A useful rule is to close the most recently opened element first. If you open a paragraph and then a strong element, close strong before closing the paragraph. Think of nested elements as containers: the inner container should be completed before the outer container ends.

Some elements are void elements, which means they do not wrap content and do not have closing tags. Examples include img for images, br for a line break, and meta for document metadata. You write an img element with its attributes in one tag; you do not add a separate </img> tag. By contrast, p, h1, and strong normally have closing tags. Knowing which pattern an element uses prevents common beginner errors.

blocks.text: The image in this example uses a file called book.png. If that file does not exist at the expected location, the browser cannot display that image. The alt text provides a text alternative. This illustrates an important point: valid markup does not guarantee that every referenced file exists. The HTML can be structurally correct while an image fails to load because its path is wrong or the file is missing.

blocks.question: You want the phrase 'read carefully' to be strongly important inside a paragraph. Which implementation uses nesting correctly?
options: Read carefully.
Read carefully.
Read carefully

Read

carefully.
blocks.explanation: The strong element is opened inside the paragraph and closed before the paragraph closes. The other choices close elements in the wrong order or include an extra closing tag.
blocks.hint: Close the inner element before closing its parent.

blocks.text: Section 4 — Attributes and the complete document

An attribute supplies extra information about an element. It appears in the opening tag, usually as a name followed by an equals sign and a quoted value. For example, class="intro" assigns a class name, href="about.html" gives a link its destination, and src="book.png" tells an image where its file is located. Attributes do not replace the element; they configure or describe it. Different elements support different attributes, and some attributes have special meaning across many elements.

Consider the anchor element, written as <a>. It creates a link, but the href attribute normally tells the browser where that link should navigate. An href value may point to another website, a page in the same project, or a location within the current page. An image uses src to identify its image resource. Its alt attribute provides a text alternative describing the image's purpose or content. Good alt text helps people using screen readers and can also help when an image cannot load.

Now let's assemble a proper HTML document. The doctype declaration tells the browser to use modern HTML parsing mode. The html element wraps the document. The head element contains information about the document, such as its title, character encoding, and viewport settings. The body element contains the content intended to appear in the page. This separation is important: a browser tab title belongs in head, while the main visible heading belongs in body.

The lang attribute on the html element identifies the main language of the document, such as en for English. The charset metadata commonly uses UTF-8, which supports a broad range of characters. The viewport metadata helps mobile browsers lay out the page at the device width rather than treating the screen as a much wider desktop layout. The title element names the document and often supplies the text shown in the browser tab. These details make a document more reliable and usable.

blocks.title: Sample 4 — A complete first webpage
blocks.code:
Welcome to My Page

I am learning to build websites.

My Goal

I will practise HTML and improve step by step.

Learn more about HTML

My first HTML project
blocks.output: A webpage with a main heading, introductory paragraph, goal section, documentation link, and footer.

blocks.text: Read the complete example from top to bottom. The doctype comes first. The html element contains head and body. Inside head are metadata and the document title. Inside body are header, main, and footer regions. The header introduces the page, main contains its primary content, and footer contains supporting information. These semantic elements help describe the role of each region. The browser can display a basic HTML page without them, but they are useful choices for a well-organised document.

blocks.question: Your page displays the main heading correctly, but the browser tab shows no useful document title. Which change addresses the problem while keeping the visible heading in the right place?
options: Put the visible h1 inside head and place the title element inside body.
Add a second body element and place the title inside it.
Put the title element inside the main element so it replaces the heading.
Add a meaningful title element inside head and keep the visible h1 inside body.
blocks.explanation: The title element belongs in head and supplies the document's title. The h1 is a visible heading and belongs in the body content. They serve different purposes and should not be swapped.
blocks.hint: One element names the document; the other labels the main visible content.

blocks.text: Section 5 — Think like a developer and practise independently

A developer does not only type code; a developer observes results, identifies causes, and tests improvements. When your page does not look as expected, do not immediately rewrite everything. First inspect the exact tag names, opening and closing tags, quotation marks, nesting, and file paths. Ask yourself what you expected the browser to do and what actually happened. Compare those two things, change one likely cause, and test again. This method makes debugging more systematic.

Suppose a link looks like ordinary text and does not navigate. Check whether you wrote an anchor element and supplied a useful href value. Suppose an image is missing. Check the spelling and location of the file referenced by src, then check whether the alt text describes the image. Suppose your heading appears in the browser tab rather than in the page. Check whether you used title when you meant h1. Many beginner problems become easier once you identify the specific job each element performs.

Let's practise the complete process. Open your editor and create a file named index.html. Type the document structure from Sample 4. Change the title to your own project title, write a main heading, add two paragraphs, and include one link to a resource you trust. Save the file and open it in your browser or the HTML preview. Then change the heading and save again. Observe how the browser reflects your edit. You have now experienced the basic authoring cycle: write, save, preview, inspect, and improve.

Before finishing, remember that HTML is not about making every page look identical. It is about giving content an appropriate structure. Two pages can use the same elements and look very different once CSS is applied. Similarly, JavaScript can make one page respond to user actions while another remains mostly static. Learn the structure first, and you will have a much stronger foundation when you later study styling, forms, responsive layouts, and interactive applications.

blocks.question: You save index.html and open it, but the image is missing. The image element is . Which is the best first debugging step?
options: Add a closing </img> tag because every HTML element must have one.
Check that the file exists at the expected images/logo.png path relative to the HTML file and that its spelling matches.
Move the alt text into the title element so the browser can find the image.
Replace img with h1 because headings automatically load local image files.
blocks.explanation: The src attribute points to the image resource. The browser must be able to find a file at that path, including the correct folder and filename. An img element is void and does not require a closing tag; alt text does not locate the file.
blocks.hint: The markup can be correct while the referenced file path is wrong.

blocks.text: Your first milestone

Excellent work. You have covered the core ideas behind a first HTML page: browsers interpret HTML, elements give content meaning, tags mark the boundaries of many elements, nesting creates relationships, attributes supply extra information, and a complete document separates head information from body content. You have also seen how to reason about missing images, link destinations, and document titles. These are practical skills, not just definitions.

Before moving to Lesson 2, challenge yourself to create a small personal profile page without copying Sample 4 line by line. Include a document title, a main heading, at least two paragraphs, a subsection heading, and one working link. Add an image only if you have a valid image file and provide meaningful alt text. If something fails, debug it patiently. In the next lesson, you will focus on HTML text and headings and learn how to organise written content into a clearer hierarchy.
